OK, so what is Ballybin trying to do now?  I've assumed that it
essentially is returning a clean version of what it found on the tape,
spaces and all.  Now there are plenty of cases where it doesn't
succeed.  As can be seen from the report, version 2 in particular is
quite unstable.  And the older versions often break up a single load
into multiple loads.  But there are lots of cases where Ballybin
successfully returns a long load followed by a short burst (such as
General Video Assembler code), as well as cases where it returns
several loads separated by long spaces (such as the George Moses music
compilations).  So I've been thinking of the problems we encounter as
issues of implementation rather than design.  Is there something more
to it?

Paul

3001:
Paul wrote:
>>
So I've been thinking of the problems we encounter as issues of implementation rather than design.  Is there something more to it?
>>

Ballybin "understands" the way that Bally BASIC writes to tape and so it knows what to "expect" when it is reading a WAV file.  If it doesn't get what it expects, then it won't work.  Early versions of Ballybin used to run into problems quite frequently.  For each new "glitch" the program had to be changed to "expect" a certain result coming in from the WAV file.  This gives much greater control over the arrangement of the output WAV file, but it means that Ballybin has to "understand" what is going on.  If Ballybin could generate a RAW file, then it would look at a "one" or a "zero" coming in from the input WAV file and just output a "one" or a "zero."  Ballybin wouldn't have to understand ANYTHING at all, but this limits the flexability of the program.  For instance, you wouldn't be able to change header or footer size.  However, as I've said before, it could prove of benefit in the future, especially as we begin to unearth programs saved in strange ways.  Ideally, every time Ballybin crashes it would be nice to have it updated, but that's certainly not realistic.

By the way, if Bob wrote a version of Ballybin300 that only output a RAW file (because he didn't have the inclination, time, motivation, or whatever to figure-out how 300-BAUD works), then the output file would still be FAR smaller when it was zipped.  Also RAW files of 300-BAUD tapes make even more sense because there were so many experimental ways that people came up with to save their 300-BAUD programs that it might be near impossible to track them all down and figure them all out.

Adam
3002:
Top Ten Astrocade Games
(May 1, 2006)
By Adam Trionfo

There are FAR, FAR less games for the Astrocade than other consoles (if you dismiss the tape games).  If you had to make a top ten list of CARTRIDGE titles, in order of preference, what would be your games of choice?  Here is my list (with a BRIEF explanation as to why) :


1) Astro BASIC - It gives you access to SO much more software.  Even if you never have programmed in your life, you can load other peoples work and check it out.

2) Dogpatch  Super simple, yet fun.  Too bad it is two-player only.  I wish that I could play this well on the emulator with the mouse, but it just is unplayable.  That seems to be the case with paddle games for many emulators.

3) Space Fortress  Easy to learn.  Hard to master.  The Astrocade hand-controller works quite well with this.

4) Scribbling  With two players, this game is fun; with four human players it is fantastic.

5) Artillery Duel  Simple and silly.  A one-player version of this would be boring.  It is the look of anticipation as the bomb drops on your opponent that makes this great!  Is the bomb going to hit or just barely miss?  I could do without the introduction every time.  Its cool once or twice, but it gets old quickly (and its time consuming).

6) Ms. Candyman  A great semi-original game.  If Muncher werent just Pac-Man, then it would be here instead.

7) The Incredible Wizard  Another great game that is okay with one-player, but REALLY shines with two people.  Stabbing people in the back is part of the fun of this game!

8) Galactic Invasion  This is Galaxian.  It has great graphics for the Astrocade.  Also it is FAR better than Astro Battle (aka, Space Invaders).

9) Treasure Cove  Fun.  The idea of using the joystick button for speed adds to the game.  Great, colorful graphics.

10) Life  This isnt a game, but I guess I like the pretty pictures  Really, sit down with the instructions for this and just try it out.  Youll enjoy it (and may even learn something too).  Leave your Astrocade (or emulator) on for awhile and check out what happens.  I know, there are faster modern versions, but this version, to me, beats the crap out of modern versions that are finished in seconds.  Also, I like that the colors fade away when they die.


Of the ten games Ive listed, only two are original to this system (Ms. Candyman and Treasure Cove), the other eight have versions that can be played elsewhere.  However, Dogpatch is superior to the arcade version and Life is better here than anywhere else.  As for the other games, you can find better versions on other (later) systems or in the arcade.  Its too bad that there werent more original cartridge games.  However, there was a TON of original BASIC software, and one of these days there ought to be a top ten list of THAT!

So, go ahead, send your lists, with explanations if you can.  Many people intertwine favorite games with memories of them... so send those in too.  When I get the time, I'll make an article with reader contributions for Ballyalley.com
3003:
Ok here is my shot at this...

1. Basic -  while I never would call myself a master at this.  This was my first computer that I learned to program on.  It was awesome in its day.  I remember writing some program that made alternating boxes slightly larger then the last.  starting with several seed boxes located at different parts of the screen made some prety interesting effects.  Kind of like a simple scribble running by itself.

2. Football - it was amazing how the controller made this game more interesting.  Nobody at the time had a joystick and knob controller working in the same game.  Also there is a glitch on this game if you can get your 2 defensive men overlapping on the screen you could really make up some ground on the receivers.  I used play this with dad for hours.

3. Space Fortress - Truly addictive game play and better then the arcade version, Space Zap!

4. The incredible Wizard - A game that was as good as the arcade.  Truly impressive for it's day!

5. Galactic Invasion - Very intense for a home console machine in it's day.  Just turn the skill level to 9 and keep up.  There were probably more movement on this game then anything else in it's day.

6. Artillery Duel - What else can be said this was a program that started off as a basic game and was released as a cartridge.  That was very rare for a game to do.  I believe this was also released on other computers but I think it was an original game for the old Bally.

7. Scribble -  this was the inspiration for my start in programing!

8. Pirates Chase -  about the last cartridge that I was able to get my hands on.  While it might have lacked in graphics the gameplay was extremely fun and fast for it's day!  If I remember correctly I think this was billed as one of the fastest games in its day

9. Pinball -  Absolutely without a doubt the best console version of Pinball in its day.  The use of 2 controllers was absolute brilliance for its time.

10. 280 zzap/ dodgem - This was as good or better then the arcade versions!

honorable mention goes to Munchman - while never officially released it was available and it kicked the doors off of the atari version, no comparison.  It was a shame that Bally was to scared to market it properly.

This discussion makes me realize that I haven't played enough
cartridge games.  I think I've at least started everything up in an
emulator, but I definitely haven't really gotten a feel for

1.  AstroBASIC / Bally BASIC.  This is definitely the cartridge I've

especially good.

4.  Treasure Cove.  Probably the best graphics of any game on the
system, and a fun concept as well.

5.  Pirate's Chase.  Fun and fast paced.

6.  Tornado Baseball / Tennis / Hockey / Handball.  Good use of the
paddles, and multiplayer support.

7.  Ms. Candyman.  An interesting take on the maze game genre, with
great animations.

8.  Artillery Duel.  Best use of physics in an Astrocade game.

9.  Sneaky Snake.  A very competent Centipede clone.

10.  Gunfight.  This makes great use of the controller--move with the
joystick and aim with the paddle.

Ballybin Bug Report
by Paul Thacker
May 4, 2006



Introduction

This report details some of the difficulties I've encountered when
using Ballybin and Astrowav.  I focus on the most recent iteration,
version 2 beta, but also reference version 1.4 and version 1.2 in
cases where these work better than the current version.  To ensure
consistency, I will include the versions I've used for testing, along
with .bat files I used to speed the processing.  For each version,
there is a batch-l1.bat file and a batch-l3.bat file.  Each calls
Ballybin to process every .wav file in the current directory, then
calls Astrowav to process every .bin/.bml file in the current
directory.  The only difference is that batch-l1.bat uses the -l1
option in Ballybin and batch-l3.bat uses the -l3 option.  Each file
referenced as an example is also included.

There are five major sections.  First, I discuss a problem converting
human-written .bml files to .wav files with Astrowav.  Then, I mention
a problem in decoding to BASIC discovered by Lance.  Next, I give
several examples of recordings that can't be processed with any
version of Ballybin.  It would be particularly good to get these
working, as there are no other known sources.  Next, I mention some
files that have been processed, but don't work correctly in the
current version.  These should be good for finding bugs, as the
recordings are proven to be good enough to make processing possible.
Finally, some desired additional features are mentioned.



Section 1:  BML conversion bug--

If you create a .bml file by hand and then run Astrowav v2 on it, the
resulting file can be very short and not allow the end of program
pointer to be set when loading.  In the example I created, if you run
the program, then list it, the comment on the first line is
overwritten.  See message #2536 in the Bally Alley group for more
details.  Example files:

weird_(hand_written)_[tim_hays].bml
weird_(no_end_of_program_pointer)_[tim_hays].wav



Section 2:  Problems decoding to BASIC

Lance mentioned having trouble decoding to BASIC with the command
"ballybin -d1 filename".  I believe there were several instances, but
I haven't tested this option very thoroughly.  On example is Frog Leap
version 2, which produces a .bml file that looks good at first, then
has a bunch of junk at the end without ever closing the basic tag.
Example:

frog_leap_(v2)_[ben_and_dave_ibach].wav



Section 3:  Recordings that won't process at all--

It seems that programs requiring a system with 16K or 32K RAM
expansion won't process correctly.  A large quantity of data is
processed, then the program crashes, regardless of what version is
used.  Examples:

pro_golf_(16K)_(raw)_[henry_sopko].wav
beatles_music_(minus_8_days_a_week)_(16K)_(raw)_[geroge_moses].wav
beatles_music_(32K)_(raw)_[geroge_moses].wav

Lance's recording of Sicko Therapy Session II won't process correctly
in any version of Ballybin I've tried.  Version 2 says it has a bad
stop bit.  Example:

sicko_therapy_session_ii_(raw)_[new_image].wav

RND Art I won't process correctly in any version of Ballybin.
Ballybin version 2 fails to halt.  This is particularly odd because
the raw recording will load perfectly.  Example:

rnd_art_i_(raw)_[new_image].wav

Mike White sent two versions of Lookout For The Bull.  The first one
won't process correctly.  Often there seems to be a problem in a
second, short load.  Ballybin version 2 fails to halt.  Example:

lookout_for_the_bull_(v1_from_mike_white)_(raw)_[wavemakers].wav

Some 2000 baud recordings from Russ Perry, Jr.'s tape collection won't
process correctly.  A recording Adam named written_for_brett won't
process at all in version 2 (with the -l3 option it fails to halt,
with -l1 it encounters a bad stop bit).  In other versions it will
apparently process, but the resulting program crashes when you load
it.  One of four early versions of ICBM Attack won't run after
processing in any version of Ballybin.  (The others work OK in at
least one version.)  Version 2 says it has a bad stop bit.  It's
possible this version simply isn't in a playable state.  Note that
ICBM Attack should be loaded with :RUN.  Examples:

written_for_brett_(raw).wav
icbm_attack_(v3)_(raw)_[brett_bilbrey].wav

A recording from Dave Ibach's tape collection looks like it should
have two loads, but only the first one will process in any version of
Ballybin.  I believe it is code intended to be loaded into the General
Video Assembler.  Such recordings have a fairly long load followed by
an extremely short load.  In this case, the second load on the tape is
very distorted and might not be recoverable.  Example:

all_machine_instruction_p1_(raw).wav

Several recordings from Dave Ibach's tape collection won't process at
all, but I'm not even sure that some of these have data in them.
They're generally quite short, but that might mean they're programs
assembled with the General Video Assembler.  In version 2, with either
the -l1 or -l3 option, all of these fail to halt except Assembler
Unknown 1, which has a synchronization error.  Examples:

all_machine_instruction_p14_(raw).wav
all_machine_instruction_p19_(raw).wav
assembler_unknown_1_(raw).wav
bug_puzzle_number_2_p3_(raw).wav
frog_leap_p6_(raw).wav

Lance made several recordings from some of the Astrobugs tapes that he
couldn't process.  Any version of Ballybin will process about 2000
bytes from The Collatz Conjecture (which seems a bit low).  The
resulting file crashes when loaded.  There's a second recording of
this which works much the same except version 2 says there's a bad
stop bit.  Lance made two recordings of She Loves You, and I can't get
either to work.  The first recording encounters a bad stop bit in
version 2, and will process to an unplayable file in some other
versions.  With the second recording, version 2 also processes to an
unplayable file.  The programs on Astrobugs Tape 2 have been processed
separately, but I think the entire tape needs to be processed together
to get the file searching program working correctly.  Right now,
version 2 fails to halt with the -l3 option and has a bad stop bit
with the -l1 option.  Version 1.4 with the -l1 option comes closest to
working, but crashes if you search past the first program.  Examples:

collatz_conjecture,_the_(raw_1)_[jim_dunson].wav
collatz_conjecture,_the_(raw_2)_[jim_dunson].wav
she_loves_you_(raw_1)_[george_moses].wav
she_loves_you_(raw_2)_[george_moses].wav
astrobugs_tape_2_(raw).wav



Section 4:  Recordings that have been processed, but demonstrate bugs
in Ballybin version 2--

Lance's recording of Alien Invasion won't process in Ballybin v2,
failing to halt with the -l3 option and giving a bad stop bit with the
-l1 option.  I processed it with v1.2 and the -l1 option, but there
may be a small glitch where it displays a question mark after loading
the title screen.  Example:

alien_invasion_(raw)_[l&m_software].wav

Both 2-4K Segment files from Russ's collection crash Ballybin when
using the -l1 option and make it fail to halt when using the -l3
option.  These seem to process correctly in v1.4, but I believe they
require a RAM expansion to run.  There is a very similar problem with
the 300 to 2000 baud conversion program (not sure how this works) and
the Bally Machine Load program (not sure what this is).  An extremely
short recording called joystick+stuff (not sure what this is)
encounters identical problems in version 2 and has a synchronization
error in version 1.4.  In version 1.2 it will process, but doesn't
seem to do anything.  An early version of ICBM Attack will process in
every version except 2, in which it fails to halt.  Note that this
program should be loaded with :RUN.  Examples:

2-4k_segments_1_and_2_(input (24576))_(raw).wav
2-4k_segments_1_and_2_(input (24576))_side_2_(raw).wav
300-2000_baud_conversion_routine_(raw).wav
bally_machine_load_(raw).wav
joystick+stuff_(raw).wav
icbm_attack_(v1)_(raw)_[brett_bilbrey].wav

The recordings I made from Dave Ibach's tape collection tended not to
process very well with Ballybin version 2.  I got much better results
with older versions, particularly version 1.2.  With a recording of
Avalanche, version 2 fails to halt with the -l3 option and only
partially decodes the data with the -l1 option, producing a file that
crashes when loaded.  If you use Ballybin v1.2 with the -l3 option,
you get a good output file.  Hang Up has similar problems.  In version
2, the -l3 option gives a bad stop bit and the -l1 option fails to
halt.  But if you use the -l1 option in v1.2, you get good output.
Candy Man always causes version 2 to fail to halt.  Some of the other
versions have problems with the timing between loads.  You can get a
playable program using v1.2, but the timing still seems like it might
be a little off, as there's a rather long pause between the first and
second load.  Examples:

avalanche_(raw)_[steve_walters].wav
hang_up_(raw)_[steve_walters].wav
candy_man_(raw)_[l&m_software].wav

A somewhat different problem from Dave Ibach's collection occurs with
BUG Puzzle #2 Solution.  Ballybin version 2 fails to halt on it.  The
other versions will process it, but there will be a glitch at the very
end of loading it, with AstroBASIC giving a "WHAT?" message.  However,
if you run the program anyway, it appears to work OK.  It's possible
this is an error in the program itself.  Example:

bug_puzzle_2_solution_(raw)_[ben_and_dave_ibach].wav

Often, Ballybin has difficult recognizing that some of the General
Video Assembler recordings have two loads.  Pass II recorded from Mike
White's compilation tape makes Ballybin fail to halt in version 2, and
in the older versions, only the first load is recognized.  Example:

general_video_assembler_pass_ii_(raw).wav



Section 5:  Feature requests--

The most wanted feature is definitely 300 baud support.  We now have a
large collection of 300 baud recordings, but some won't load
correctly, and even the ones that do take up a large amount of space.
 Ideally, 2000 and 300 baud support would be integrated together.
Then we could easily convert between the formats, at least for
BASIC-only programs.

Another suggestion is a raw mode that would return the exact binary
data and spacing from a recording rather than analyzing the way the
data is encoded.  This might prove useful for programs that Ballybin
has trouble processing, particularly if we find recordings that encode
data in novel ways.

I have been toying with the idea for several months of building a
multi-platform game development system. I was mailnly interested in
consoles which have a true expansion interface like the Bally,
Colecovision and Sega Master System, etc. By true expansion interface
I mean most if not all address, data and control signals. These three
consoles also have a common processor, the Z-80 which I have worked
with since the eighties. I wanted something more that just a simple
multicart with a download port. So I designed this platform with its
own processor and shared memory interface to the target console. This
allows me to take control of the target address/data bus utilizing
BUSREQ and BUSAK of the Z-80. Also I have a large expandable
multibanked flash capability using the two 40 pin module sockets.
The platform having its own processor also means that I can diagnose
and repair defective consoles. (assuming that at least the Z-80
works). The processor I use is the the Atmel Mega128 with the Bascom
AVR compiler. It does not have to be code compatible with the target
since the target console is basically shared memory & IO. I can now
write test routines for any memory or I/O device. The Bally may be
more difficult because of the custom video chips. This Bascom AVR
compiler source code would be open source and available to all to
encourage a large database of software. What do you think?

Astro Basic is the upgraded version of Bally Basic, sporting the 2000 baud cassette port on the cart.

Both Basics are interpreters.

Now, as the 4K ram in the Bally comprises the ram required to display the screen there is no extra ram to hold Basic tokens, variables or arrays. So Basic first sets 2 of the 4 colours to the same values as the other 2, then uses the alternate bits of each ram byte to hold the basic tokens and array data.

That is a byte of ram looks something like this in Basic:

GBGBGBGB

Where G is graphic image and B is Basic code.
As such it takes 2 bytes ram to hold 1 byte of basic code.

Wow, it's been quiet here lately.  So, I figured I'd give some news
about what I've been working on.  Ian loaned me his collection of
Esoterica tapes, which turns out to include most of Esoterica's
commercial releases.  Included are:

Super Sloap
Road Toad
The Great American Jigsaw & Big City Slick
Mini Golf & Starship Command
Ten Pins & Garbersville
Treasure Island & 'Fox & Hounds'
Bomb Squad & Wildcatter

The format of the tapes is interesting.  Super Slope and Road Toad are
the only machine language programs, and are 2000 baud only.  But the
other tapes include both 2000 and 300 baud versions on the same tape,
repeated on each side.  So, for example, one side would include Fox &
Hounds in 2000 baud, then Fox & Hounds in 300 baud, then Treasure
Island in 2000 baud, then Treasure Island in 300 baud.  The opposite
side has the exact same recordings, but starting with Treasure Island.
 (Some of the other tapes instead have both 2000 baud programs
followed by both 300 baud programs.)  This redundancy is definitely
helpful for archiving, and probably made it easier for the original
user to find the programs.

At this point, I have a working 2000 baud version of every unarchived
program, but still want to look at the 300 baud versions.  Also, I
need to make some scans.  The first three tapes I listed actually
include boxes and instructions.  I'd never even seen an original
Astrocade cassette box before!  So, interesting things are coming up.
 I'll give more details when I'm ready to upload everything.

> That depends.

After talking with other game collectors in Canada, it has come to my attention, that the Bally was never Officially released in Canada. There was just an unofficial distributor here in Toronto. Though he was successful in getting many stores to carry the Bally here.

Officially released in Canada products MUST have both English and French on the boxes and manuals. So, when reprinting, the 'English' spellings would be used.

However, proper names would not need to be changed. Nor programming commands. Which could lead to some interesting paragraphs in the graphics section of a manual...

However, of late. many US companies have been just taking the US product and re-wrapping it with a French/English wrapper under which is a French manual, over top of the original US shrink wrap.

Also some products just never shipped to Quebec and again retained the US spellings.

So, we regularly see a mix of US and English spellings.

3227:
My experience in the past with these systems turned up some fairly common problems to look for.

1. POWER supply failure....yes they do burn out and they could now
   be as old as 24-28 years.

2. The ON/OFF switch is subject to failure. If it works
   intermittently, this is the likely culprit.

3. The CARTRIDGE port has pins that can become corroded and require a
   good cleaning.
   (This can be easily caused by COCKROACHES which leave a corrosive
   agent secreted by the cockroach onto your metal components. They
   like the heat in electronics and tend to move inside of them.)
   A pencil eraser, (Sharpening type) will do the job.
   Rub them gently in one direction. (Dust also will cause problems.)
   Clean up all residue from the machine. Also, the card edge
   connection on the carts themselves are subject to this problem.

3b. The cartridges themselves may be defective.

4. The PLUG IN IC's get corrosion problems and will loosen due to the
   heating and cooling of components.
   Use a small screwdriver to loosene one end, then the other to
   prevent bent pins due to popping up on only one side.
   Use the eraser to gently clean the pins on the IC's.
   (If they have been removed previously, look underneath for bent
    pins.)
   IMPORTANT: Make sure the polarity notch of the IC is lined
   up with the notch on the socket and all pins are straight and all
   pins enter their respective holes.

5. The RF MODULATOR box is a plug in unit. These can also fail.
   (This is the TV output unit.)

5b. Check you have the channel selector set for the correct channel.

   I hope this helps.
